Derived Parameters with Standard Errors and Intervals

Source: R/derived_estimates.R
derived_estimates.Rd

Estimates functions of a fitted model's parameters – a sum of two coefficients, a difference, a probability built from several of them – each with a standard error, a z test against zero and a confidence interval. The parameters are named by the labels wald_test() uses.

Usage

derived_estimates(fit, ..., level = 0.95, se = c("robust", "hessian", "opg"))

Arguments

fit

A model wald_test() accepts.

...

Named derived parameters: weight vectors or functions (see Details).

level

Confidence level of the intervals.

se

For growth models, which covariance estimator to use, as in wald_test(). Ignored otherwise.

Value

A data frame with one row per derived parameter: parameter, estimate, se, z, p, lower, upper.

Details

Each derived parameter is given as one named argument in ..., either

  • a named numeric vector of weights, c(a = 1, b = 1, c = -1), meaning \(a + b - c\); its variance is \(c^\top V c\), exact; or

  • a function of the named vector of estimates, returning one number, such as function(p) plogis(p[["a"]] + p[["b"]]). Its standard error is the delta method's, \(\sqrt{g^\top V g}\) with \(g\) the gradient of the function at the estimates, taken by central differences.

\(V\) is the covariance matrix the fit reports (for a growth model, the one se selects). The interval is the estimate plus or minus the normal quantile times the standard error, on the scale of the derived parameter. For a probability near 0 or 1 an interval built on the logit scale and transformed back stays inside the unit interval; derive the logit, and transform its bounds with plogis().

For fit_joint_classes() the labels are those of joint_coefficients(): "Y#j Intercept", "Y#j ON X#k", "Y#j ON w" and "Y#j ON w | X#k". A covariate w acting on y by x class has slope "Y#j ON w" in the last x class and that plus "Y#j ON w | X#k" in class k, so the association among cases with w = 1 is c("Y#j ON X#k" = 1, "Y#j ON w | X#k" = 1). joint_probabilities() builds the conditional class probabilities this way.

References

Oehlert, G. W. (1992). A note on the delta method. The American Statistician, 46(1), 27-29.

See also

wald_test() to test several restrictions at once, joint_probabilities().

Examples

# \donttest{
set.seed(1)
n  <- 800
w  <- rbinom(n, 1, 0.5)
cx <- sample(1:2, n, TRUE)
cy <- ifelse(runif(n) < plogis(-1 + 2 * (cx == 1) + w * (cx == 1)), 1L, 2L)
A  <- sapply(1:4, function(j) rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(cx == 1, 0.85, 0.15)))
S  <- sapply(1:4, function(j) rbinom(n, 1, ifelse(cy == 1, 0.85, 0.15)))
fit <- fit_joint_classes(A, S, predictors_y = data.frame(w = w),
                         y_effects = "by_x", n_init = 5, random_state = 1)
# The association among cases with w = 1, and the probability of y class 1
# for x class 1 at w = 1.
derived_estimates(fit,
  assoc_w1 = c("Y#1 ON X#1" = 1, "Y#1 ON w | X#1" = 1),
  p_w1 = function(p) plogis(p[["Y#1 Intercept"]] + p[["Y#1 ON X#1"]] +
                            p[["Y#1 ON w"]] + p[["Y#1 ON w | X#1"]]))
#>   parameter  estimate        se         z            p     lower    upper
#> 1  assoc_w1 2.9233534 0.3441608  8.494149 1.993885e-17 2.2488106 3.597896
#> 2      p_w1 0.6976749 0.0393972 17.708741 3.590148e-70 0.6204578 0.774892
# }
